raw_case_text:
A 31-year-old man with no relevant medical history was treated in the internal medicine department of our hospital. He reported a history of poorly defined malaise, night sweats, sleeplessness, tinnitus, and episodic diarrhea with no pathologic products during the previous 6 days. He did not report fever, chills, or headache. Two weeks earlier, he had spent 10 days in Puerto Plata in a tourist resort, without traveling to any other place. He had not received any antimalarial chemoprophylaxis. Physical examination showed no abnormalities. Laboratory values, including levels of sodium, potassium, liver enzymes, creatinine, and coagulation factors, as well as results of hemogram and chest radiograph, were within normal limits. A blood film showed trophozoytes of P. vivax and P. malariae. In a stool specimen, Entamoeba histolytica, Trichiuris trichura, Endolimax nana, and Blastocystis hominis were observed; stool cultures were negative.
Treatment was initiated with chloroquine (4 doses) and primaquine for a period of 14 days; metronidazole and paromomycin were administered for the intestinal infestations. Symptoms resolved in 48 hours, and control blood films showed clearance of the parasitemia. Two months after the end of treatment, the patient remained asymptomatic.
We describe a new and unusual case of imported vivax-malariae malaria. Two characteristics of our patient's case bear mention. First, the place of acquisition of the infection and the species of Plasmodium involved are notable. The Dominican Republic is considered a low-risk area for malaria, although some places in the west, on the Haitian border, are malaria-endemic. In addition, according to available information, autochthonous malaria cases increased after Hurricane George (3,003 cases in 1999, compared to 2,000 in 1998). Previously described sporadic cases of imported malaria from the Dominican Republic included those in tourists who traveled to Punta Cana, in the eastern part of the country. All these cases were caused by P. falciparum. To our knowledge, no cases of P. vivax or mixed P. vivax/P. malariae infection have been described after travel to the Dominican Republic. From January 1999 to September 2003, TropNetEurop (a European surveillance network of tropical and imported diseases) noted 618 cases of P. vivax infection imported to Europe. The most common areas of acquisition of P. vivax infection were the Indian subcontinent (17%), Indonesia (12.1%), South America (11.4%), and West Africa (11.4%). Only 0.2% of the cases of P. vivax infection were acquired in the Caribbean, none of them in the Dominican Republic.
Second, the clinical features were atypical. Malaria usually starts as a febrile syndrome, accompanied by chills, headache, malaise, and arthromyalgia. However, sometimes symptoms are unspecific. In fact <10% of patients do not exhibit fever or chills, and some report only poorly defined complaints or other atypical symptoms. Among these, gastrointestinal symptoms are the most frequently reported. In the present case, the syndrome could have been easily explained by the intestinal infestations detected in stool studies, and malaria would have been overlooked if the clinician had not taken into account this disease in the diagnostic workup.
In summary, clinicians should include malaria in the diagnostic workup of tourists who become ill after traveling to the Dominican Republic. Species other than P. falciparum may be the cause of the disease; these species likely induce more atypical forms of malaria.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 31-year-old male presenting with malaise, night sweats, insomnia, tinnitus, and episodic diarrhea of six days' duration.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 31-year-old male presented with a six-day history of poorly defined malaise, night sweats, sleeplessness, tinnitus, and episodic watery diarrhea without blood or mucus. Symptoms began two weeks following a 10-day vacation at a tourist resort in Puerto Plata, Dominican Republic. He specifically did not experience fever, chills, or headache, and had not taken chemoprophylaxis.
subjective.past_medical_history: Returned 2 weeks prior from a 10-day stay in Puerto Plata, Dominican Republic, without travel to other regions. No antimalarial chemoprophylaxis taken. No relevant past medical history.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for malaise, night sweats, insomnia, tinnitus, and episodic non-bloody diarrhea. Negative for fever, chills, rigors, headache, nausea, or vomiting. Medications: none. Allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Afebrile, hemodynamically stable. Physical examination showed no abnormalities; no pallor, jaundice, lymphadenopathy, abdominal tenderness, or hepatosplenomegaly.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count, serum sodium, potassium, liver transaminases, serum creatinine, and coagulation tests were within normal limits. Chest radiograph: normal. Stool microscopy: demonstrated Entamoeba histolytica, Trichuris trichiura, Endolimax nana, and Blastocystis hominis; stool bacterial cultures were negative. Peripheral blood film performed.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Atypical afebrile co-infection with Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium malariae (imported mixed malaria from the Dominican Republic) with concurrent intestinal polyparasitism (Entamoeba histolytica, Trichuris trichiura, Endolimax nana, and Blastocystis hominis).
Diagnostic confirmation: Peripheral blood film revealing trophozoites of Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium malariae; stool examination identifying intestinal protozoa and helminths with sterile stool cultures.
Treatment & Outcome: Treated with oral chloroquine (4 doses) followed by primaquine for 14 days for radical cure; concurrent intestinal parasites treated with oral metronidazole and paromomycin. All symptoms resolved within 48 hours, follow-up blood films confirmed clearance of parasitemia, and the patient remained asymptomatic at two months post-treatment.
